concept.title: Digit Sum Formula for Prime Reciprocals with Half-Order Periods
concept.concept_description: For a prime p ≥ 3 and an integer b ≥ 2 with p ∤ b, if the multiplicative order of b modulo p is l = (p-1)/2^m and p ≡ 1 mod 2^(m+1), then the sum of the base-b digits in one full period of the expansion of 1/p equals (b-1)(p-1)/2^(m+1).
concept.mathematical_framing: For a prime p ≥ 3 and an integer b ≥ 2 with p ∤ b, if the multiplicative order of b modulo p is l = (p-1)/2^m and p ≡ 1 mod 2^(m+1), then the sum of the base-b digits in one full period of the expansion of 1/p equals (b-1)(p-1)/2^(m+1).
concept.lean_guess: Define the base-b digit sequence of 1/p using the division algorithm on remainders, a_i = ⌊b * r_i / p⌋ where r_i = b^i mod p. The sum of digits S = Σ a_i can be expressed in terms of the sum of remainders. The condition that the order of b is (p-1)/2^m restricts the remainders to a subgroup of (ℤ/pℤ)×. The congruence p ≡ 1 mod 2^(m+1) ensures that this subgroup is stable under negation modulo p (since l is even and b^(l/2) ≡ -1 mod p), which allows the sum of remainders to be simplified to p*l/2, leading directly to the formula S = (b-1)*l/2 = (b-1)(p-1)/2^(m+1).

This file exhibits an explicit, non-vacuous finite unit-distance graph in the
plane and instantiates the general `1/4` independence-ratio bound on it.

(indeed `3`-chromatic), so the headline theorem
`indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable` applies and gives independence ratio

# A concrete planar unit-distance graph meeting the `1/4` bound

This file exhibits an explicit, non-vacuous finite unit-distance graph in the
plane and instantiates the general `1/4` independence-ratio bound on it.

The three vertices of a unit equilateral triangle,
`(0,0)`, `(1,0)`, `(1/2, √3/2)`, are pairwise at Euclidean distance exactly `1`.
Hence their unit-distance graph is the complete graph `K₃`.  It is `4`-colourable
(indeed `3`-chromatic), so the headline theorem
`indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable` applies and gives independence ratio
`≥ 1/4`.  We also compute the *exact* independence ratio, `1/3`, confirming the
graph genuinely lies strictly above the `1/4` threshold.
-/
import Mathlib
import Catalog.Computation.UnitDistanceIndependenceRatio

open Finset SimpleGraph EuclideanSpace
open Catalog.Computation.UnitDistanceIndependenceRatio

namespace Catalog.Computation.EquilateralTriangleUDG

/-- The three vertices of a unit equilateral triangle in the plane. -/
noncomputable def triPoints : Fin 3 → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)
  | 0 => !₂[0, 0]
  | 1 => !₂[1, 0]
  | 2 => !₂[1 / 2, Real.sqrt 3 / 2]

/-
Any two distinct triangle vertices are at unit distance.
-/
lemma triPoints_dist_one (i j : Fin 3) (h : i ≠ j) :
    dist (triPoints i) (triPoints j) = 1 := by
  fin_cases i <;> fin_cases j <;> simp +decide [ triPoints ] at h ⊢;
  all_goals norm_num [ dist_eq_norm, EuclideanSpace.norm_eq ]; all_goals norm_num [ div_pow ]

/-
The equilateral-triangle unit-distance graph is exactly the complete graph on
three vertices: two vertices are adjacent iff they are distinct.
-/
lemma triGraph_adj_iff (i j : Fin 3) :
    (unitDistanceGraph triPoints).Adj i j ↔ i ≠ j := by
  exact ⟨ fun h => h.1, fun h => ⟨ h, triPoints_dist_one i j h ⟩ ⟩

/-
The triangle graph is `4`-colourable (in fact `3`-chromatic).
-/
lemma triGraph_colorable : (unitDistanceGraph triPoints).Colorable 4 := by
  refine' ⟨ _, _ ⟩;
  exact fun i => Fin.castLE ( by decide ) i;
  simp +decide [ triGraph_adj_iff ]

/-- **Instantiation of the headline bound.**  The concrete equilateral-triangle
unit-distance graph has an independent set of relative size at least `1/4`. -/
theorem triGraph_indep_ratio_ge_quarter :
    ∃ S : Finset (Fin 3),
      (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ (unitDistanceGraph triPoints).Adj v u) ∧
      (1 : ℝ) / 4 ≤ (S.card : ℝ) / (Fintype.card (Fin 3)) :=
  indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable (unitDistanceGraph triPoints) triGraph_colorable

/-
**Exact independence ratio.**  Every independent set of the triangle graph has
at most one vertex, and a one-vertex independent set exists; hence the exact
independence ratio is `1/3`, comfortably above the `1/4` threshold.
-/
theorem triGraph_indep_ratio_eq_third :
    (∀ S : Finset (Fin 3),
        (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ (unitDistanceGraph triPoints).Adj v u) →
        (S.card : ℝ) / (Fintype.card (Fin 3)) ≤ 1 / 3) ∧
      (∃ S : Finset (Fin 3),
        (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ (unitDistanceGraph triPoints).Adj v u) ∧
        (S.card : ℝ) / (Fintype.card (Fin 3)) = 1 / 3) := by
  constructor;
  · intro S hS;
    fin_cases S <;> simp +decide [ triGraph_adj_iff ] at hS ⊢;
  · refine' ⟨ { 0 }, _, _ ⟩ <;> norm_num

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

**Hypothesis.**  The general `1/4` bound of `UnitDistanceIndependenceRatio.lean`
should be *non-vacuous*: there is an explicit planar unit-distance graph to which
it applies, and its true ratio should sit strictly above `1/4`.

**Experiment.**  We placed the three vertices of a unit equilateral triangle at
`(0,0)`, `(1,0)`, `(1/2, sqrt 3 / 2)`.  `triPoints_dist_one` verifies all three
pairwise Euclidean distances equal `1` (the `sqrt 3 / 2` coordinate makes the
radicand collapse to `1` via `Real.sq_sqrt`).  `triGraph_adj_iff` then shows the
resulting unit-distance graph is exactly `K_3`, `triGraph_colorable` gives a
4-colouring (via an injection `Fin 3 -> Fin 4`), and
`triGraph_indep_ratio_ge_quarter` instantiates the headline bound.

**Analysis.**  `triGraph_indep_ratio_eq_third` computes the *exact* ratio: any

one vertex, so the ratio is exactly `1/3 > 1/4`.  The witness therefore lies
strictly inside the admissible region, confirming the bound is not tight here.

**Critique.**  The geometry is genuine (real square-root distance computation,
not `decide`), and the two directions of the exact-ratio theorem are both
non-trivial (an upper bound over all independent sets plus an explicit witness).

**Synthesis.**  A fully verified planar witness anchoring the abstract engine,
showing the `1/4` threshold is met with room to spare by the smallest
non-trivial planar unit-distance graph.

plane has independence ratio `α(G)/|V| ≥ 1/4`.  As the Lab Notes below record,
the *unconditional* statement is **not** a theorem that follows from planar
colourability: the plane contains 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs (de Grey,
2018), so one cannot obtain a `1/4` bound from a 4-colouring of the plane, and
the best known lower bound for the independence ratio of the plane sits *below*
`1/4`.  We therefore isolate the rigorous mathematical core and prove it in full.

## Main results

* `exists_large_colorClass` — pigeonhole: a proper `k`-colouring has a colour
  class of real size `≥ n/k`.
* `exists_indepSet_of_coloring` / `indep_of_colorable` — every `k`-colourable
  graph has an independent set `S` with `n ≤ k · |S|`.
* `indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable` — the headline `1/4` bound for the
  class of **4-colourable** unit-distance graphs (and any 4-colourable graph).
* `completeGraph_ratio_eq` — the bound `1/k` is **tight**: the complete graph
  `K_k` is `k`-colourable and has independence ratio exactly `1/k`.
* `unitDistanceGraph` — the plane unit-distance graph of a family of points.

* A. D. N. J. de Grey, "The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5" (2018).
* D. Cranston, L. Rabern, "The fractional chromatic number of the plane" (2017).

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Probability.IndependentSet

open Finset SimpleGraph

namespace Catalog.Computation.UnitDistanceIndependenceRatio

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-! ## The colouring / pigeonhole engine -/

/-
**Pigeonhole for colourings.**  If `C` is a proper `k`-colouring of a finite
graph (`k > 0`), then some colour class has real cardinality at least `n / k`,
equivalently `n ≤ k · |class|`.
-/
omit [DecidableEq V] in
lemma exists_large_colorClass (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k)
    (C : G.Coloring (Fin k)) :
    ∃ c : Fin k,
      (Fintype.card V : ℝ) ≤ k * (univ.filter (fun v => C v = c)).card := by
  have h_card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise : Fintype.card V = ∑ c : Fin k, (Finset.univ.filter (fun v => C v = c)).card := by
    simp +decide only [card_eq_sum_ones, sum_fiberwise];
    rw [ Fintype.card_eq_sum_ones ];
  have h_exists_le : ∃ c : Fin k, (Fintype.card V : ℝ) / k ≤ (Finset.univ.filter (fun v => C v = c)).card := by
    contrapose! h_card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise;
    exact ne_of_gt ( by rw [ ← @Nat.cast_lt ℝ ] ; push_cast; exact lt_of_lt_of_le ( Finset.sum_lt_sum_of_nonempty ⟨ ⟨ 0, hk ⟩, Finset.mem_univ _ ⟩ fun c _ => h_card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise c ) ( by simp +decide [ mul_div_cancel₀, hk.ne' ] ) );
  exact h_exists_le.imp fun c hc => by rwa [ div_le_iff₀' ( Nat.cast_pos.mpr hk ) ] at hc;

/-
A colour class of a proper colouring is an independent set.
-/
omit [DecidableEq V] in
lemma indep_colorClass (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ} (C : G.Coloring (Fin k)) (c : Fin k) :
    ∀ v ∈ (univ.filter (fun v => C v = c)),
      ∀ u ∈ (univ.filter (fun v => C v = c)), v ≠ u → ¬ G.Adj v u := by
  exact fun v hv u hu huv h => C.valid h ( by aesop )

/-
From a proper `k`-colouring we extract an independent set `S` with
`n ≤ k · |S|`.
-/
omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem exists_indepSet_of_coloring (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k)
    (C : G.Coloring (Fin k)) :
    ∃ S : Finset V, (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ G.Adj v u) ∧
      (Fintype.card V : ℝ) ≤ k * S.card := by
  obtain ⟨ c, hc ⟩ := exists_large_colorClass G hk C;
  exact ⟨ _, indep_colorClass G C c, hc ⟩

/-
Any `k`-colourable finite graph (`k > 0`) has an independent set `S` with
`n ≤ k · |S|`.
-/
omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem indep_of_colorable (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k)
    (hcol : G.Colorable k) :
    ∃ S : Finset V, (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ G.Adj v u) ∧
      (Fintype.card V : ℝ) ≤ k * S.card := by
  convert exists_indepSet_of_coloring G hk ( hcol.toColoring ( by simp +decide ) )

/-! ## The `1/4` bound for 4-colourable graphs -/

/-
**Headline result.**  Every 4-colourable finite graph (in particular every
4-colourable unit-distance graph) has an independent set whose relative size is
at least `1/4`; i.e. the independence ratio cannot fall below `1/4`.
-/
omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    (hcol : G.Colorable 4) :
    ∃ S : Finset V, (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ G.Adj v u) ∧
      (1 : ℝ) / 4 ≤ (S.card : ℝ) / (Fintype.card V) := by
  obtain ⟨ S, hS₁, hS₂ ⟩ := indep_of_colorable G zero_lt_four hcol;
  exact ⟨ S, hS₁, by rw [ div_le_div_iff₀ ] <;> first | positivity | norm_cast at * ; linarith ⟩

/-! ## Tightness: the complete graph attains ratio `1/k` -/

/-
In the complete graph, an independent set has at most one vertex.
-/
lemma indepSet_completeGraph_card_le_one {k : ℕ} (S : Finset (Fin k))
    (hS : ∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ (completeGraph (Fin k)).Adj v u) :
    S.card ≤ 1 := by
  exact Finset.card_le_one.mpr fun v hv u hu => Classical.not_not.1 fun h => hS v hv u hu h <| by aesop;

/-
**Sharpness of the colouring bound.**  For `k > 0`, the complete graph `K_k`
is `k`-colourable, yet every independent set has at most one vertex, so its
independence ratio is exactly `1/k`.  Hence the `1/k` lower bound proved above
cannot be improved.
-/
theorem completeGraph_ratio_eq {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k) :
    (completeGraph (Fin k)).Colorable k ∧
      (∀ S : Finset (Fin k),
        (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ (completeGraph (Fin k)).Adj v u) →
        (S.card : ℝ) / (Fintype.card (Fin k)) ≤ 1 / k) := by
  refine' ⟨ _, fun S hS => _ ⟩;
  · exact ⟨ ⟨ fun x => x, by aesop ⟩ ⟩;
  · rw [ div_le_div_iff₀ ] <;> norm_cast;
    · simp +zetaDelta at *;
      exact mul_le_of_le_one_left hk.le ( Finset.card_le_one.mpr fun x hx y hy => hS x hx y hy );
    · simpa

/-

    (hm : 0 < G.edgeFinset.card) :
    ∃ S : Finset V, (∀ v ∈ S, ∀ u ∈ S, v ≠ u → ¬ G.Adj v u) ∧

  obtain ⟨ S, hS₁, hS₂, hS₃ ⟩ := Catalog.Combinatorics.ProbabilisticMethod.exists_large_independent_set G hm;
  exact ⟨ S, hS₂, hS₃ ⟩

/-- The **unit-distance graph** of a family of points `p : ι → ℝ²`: two indices
are adjacent iff they are distinct and their points are at Euclidean distance
exactly `1`. -/
def unitDistanceGraph {ι : Type*} (p : ι → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) : SimpleGraph ι where
  Adj i j := i ≠ j ∧ dist (p i) (p j) = 1
  symm := by rintro i j ⟨h1, h2⟩; exact ⟨h1.symm, by rw [_root_.dist_comm]; exact h2⟩

/-- **Specialisation to unit-distance graphs.**  A 4-colourable finite

    (hcol : (unitDistanceGraph p).Colorable 4) :

      (1 : ℝ) / 4 ≤ (S.card : ℝ) / (Fintype.card ι) := by
  exact indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable (unitDistanceGraph p) hcol

# Computational Evidence — Minimum Independence Ratio Constraint

## 1. Small-case calculations

Independence ratio `alpha(G) / n` for standard finite unit-distance graphs:

| Graph                         | n | alpha | ratio  | >= 1/4 ? |
|-------------------------------|---|-------|--------|----------|
| single edge (K_2)             | 2 | 1     | 0.5000 | yes      |
| equilateral triangle (K_3)    | 3 | 1     | 0.3333 | yes      |
| Moser spindle                 | 7 | 2     | 0.2857 | yes      |
| Golomb graph                  | 10| 3     | 0.3000 | yes      |
| hexagonal 7-vertex wheel      | 7 | 2     | 0.2857 | yes      |

Every small explicit unit-distance graph sits comfortably above `1/4`. This is
consistent with the proven statement (`triGraph_indep_ratio_eq_third`) that the
smallest non-trivial planar witness, the unit triangle, has ratio exactly
`1/3`.

## 2. The subtlety behind the "1/4" threshold

The mission claim is that the ratio can *never* fall below `1/4`. The relevant
sequence is the **independence ratio of the plane**, i.e. the infimum over all
finite unit-distance graphs. Known bounds (density / packing arguments):

* lower bound on the maximal density of a distance-1-avoiding set: about `0.229`;
* upper bound: about `0.254`.

Because the lower endpoint `0.229 < 0.25`, the "one quarter" figure is **not**
established; it is a conjectural threshold, and current constructions leave open
the possibility that the true infimum is below `1/4`. Colouring cannot rescue
the bound: de Grey's 2018 construction gives a finite planar unit-distance graph
of chromatic number `5`, so there is no global `4`-colouring of the plane.

## 3. What is provable, and what we proved

The genuinely theorem-shaped statement is the **conditional** one:

* If a finite graph is `4`-colourable then its independence ratio is `>= 1/4`
  (`indep_ratio_ge_quarter_of_four_colorable`), by the pigeonhole
  "largest colour class" argument.
* This bound `1/k` is tight for `K_k` (`completeGraph_ratio_eq`), so `1/4` is the
  exact constant available from `4`-colourability.
* The unit equilateral triangle realises the hypotheses concretely with true
  ratio `1/3` (`triGraph_indep_ratio_eq_third`).

## 4. Counterexample hunt

No finite unit-distance graph with independence ratio below `1/4` is known, and
none was found among the small graphs above. However, the *unconditional* claim
is **not** verified here: it is equivalent to a density lower bound that current
mathematics places out of reach (the best proven lower bound is `~0.229`). We
therefore certify only the conditional (colouring-based) form and record the
gap honestly.

## 5. OEIS note

The sequence of independence numbers of the record `k`-chromatic planar
unit-distance graphs is not a clean OEIS entry; the numeric density bounds
(`0.229 ...`, `0.254 ...`) are real constants from the packing literature rather
than integer sequences, so no OEIS identifier applies.

# Future Directions — Independence Ratios of Unit-Distance Graphs

This cycle established a clean, sharp relationship between colourability and the
independence ratio of finite graphs, instantiated it on planar unit-distance
graphs, and isolated exactly where the folklore "one quarter" threshold stops
being a theorem and becomes a conjecture. The following directions are derived
directly from those findings.

## 1. The true infimum of the planar independence ratio

**Conjecture.** The infimum, over all finite unit-distance graphs in the plane,
of the ratio between a largest set of mutually non-unit-distance vertices and the
total number of vertices is a single well-defined constant strictly between
`0.22` and `0.26`, and in particular it is **strictly below one quarter**.

*The key insight is* that the "one quarter" figure is an artefact of four-colour
intuition, and colourability provably cannot deliver it: there exist finite
planar configurations requiring five colours, so the quarter bound must be argued
—if it holds at all—by a packing or density argument rather than by colouring,
and the best packing constructions already push the ceiling toward `0.229`.

*Why now?* The recent discovery of explicit five-chromatic planar
unit-distance configurations removed the last reason to expect a four-colour
proof of the quarter bound, and modern flag-algebra and linear-programming
density methods are finally sharp enough to pin the constant to two decimal
places.

## 2. Sharpness is a colouring phenomenon, not a geometric one

**Conjecture.** Among finite unit-distance graphs in the plane, the colouring
lower bound `1 / k` on the independence ratio is attained (as an equality) only
by graphs whose largest complete subgraph is a triangle, and never by a
genuinely `k`-colour-critical planar family for `k ≥ 4`.

*The key insight is* that the abstract bound `1 / k` is tight exactly on complete
graphs, but complete graphs stop being realisable by planar unit distances once
they exceed three vertices, so the geometric constraint forces every planar
witness strictly into the interior of the admissible region.

*Why now?* We have, in this cycle, both the exact tightness statement for the
abstract bound and an explicit planar triangle attaining `1 / 3`; the natural
next step is to prove that no planar family can hug the bound as `k` grows.

## 3. An edge-count phase transition for the ratio

**Conjecture.** For finite unit-distance graphs on `n` vertices with `m` edges,
the independence ratio is bounded below by a quantity of order `n / (m + n)`, and
this edge-count bound overtakes any colouring bound precisely in the sparse
regime `m = o(n^{4/3})`, which is the extremal edge count for planar unit
distances.

*The key insight is* that two entirely different mechanisms control the ratio in
different density regimes—averaging over colour classes when the graph is dense,
and the Turán/Caro–Wei degree averaging when it is sparse—and the crossover sits
exactly at the known extremal edge density for unit-distance graphs.

*Why now?* The extremal `n^{4/3}` edge bound for unit-distance graphs is
classical, but only recently have matching sparse constructions been catalogued,
making it feasible to test where the two independence-ratio mechanisms exchange
dominance.

## 4. Dimension lifts the threshold

**Conjecture.** In three-dimensional space the analogous independence-ratio
infimum is strictly smaller than in the plane, and it decays to zero as the
ambient dimension grows, at a rate governed by the exponential growth of the
kissing number.

*The key insight is* that higher dimensions permit ever larger cliques of
mutually unit-distant points (a regular simplex uses one extra dimension per
extra vertex), and each such clique drags the local independence ratio down
toward the reciprocal of the clique size.

*Why now?* Sphere-packing and kissing-number bounds were recently settled in
several key dimensions, giving, for the first time, quantitative control over how
many mutually unit-distant points a bounded region can host.

## 5. A certified separation between the fractional and integral bounds

**Conjecture.** There is an explicit finite planar unit-distance graph whose
independence ratio is strictly larger than the reciprocal of its fractional
chromatic number, exhibiting a certified gap between the fractional-colouring
prediction and the true integral ratio.

*The key insight is* that the reciprocal-fractional-chromatic-number heuristic is
only an inequality, and the slack in that inequality is itself measurable on
small critical configurations, so a single well-chosen finite graph can witness
the separation exactly.

*Why now?* Fractional chromatic numbers of small planar unit-distance graphs are
now computable to high precision, so the predicted gap can be exhibited on a
concrete, fully checkable example rather than argued asymptotically.

# Digit sum of one period of `1/p` in base `b`: the full-reptend case

successive remainders `b^k mod p` run through **all** of `{1, …, p-1}` exactly once, so
the remainder sum is `p(p-1)/2` and the digit sum of one period is `(b-1)(p-1)/2`.

This is the classical full-reptend digit-sum identity; it is the `d = p-1` sibling of the
`d = (p-1)/2` result and is proved here self-containedly.

## Proof outline

* Telescoping identity `p·D + S = b·S` (`digitSum_remSum`), identical to the half-period
  file: `b·r_k = p·a_{k+1} + r_{k+1}`, and `r_{p-1} = r_0 = 1` since `b^{p-1} ≡ 1`.
* The remainder sum equals `p(p-1)/2` (`remSum_full`): the map `k ↦ (b:ZMod p)^k` is
  injective on `range (p-1)` (order `p-1`), its image lands in the nonzero residues, and by
  a cardinality count the image is *all* nonzero residues; summing their `ZMod.val` gives
  `∑_{i<p} i = p(p-1)/2`.
* Combining, `p·D = (b-1)·S = (b-1)·p(p-1)/2`, hence `D = (b-1)(p-1)/2`.

namespace DigitSumFullPeriod

open Finset

/-- Sum of the base-`b` digits of one period (of length `d`) of `1/p`. -/
def digitSum (p b d : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, (b * (b ^ k % p)) / p

/-- Sum of the successive remainders `b^k mod p` over one period of length `d`. -/
def remSum (p b d : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, b ^ k % p

/-- Telescoping identity `p·(digit sum) + (remainder sum) = b·(remainder sum)`. -/
lemma digitSum_remSum (p b d : ℕ) (hp : 1 < p) (hd : b ^ d % p = 1) :
    p * digitSum p b d + remSum p b d = b * remSum p b d := by
  unfold digitSum remSum;
  have h_remainder : ∀ k < d, b * (b ^ k % p) = p * ((b * (b ^ k % p)) / p) + (b ^ (k + 1) % p) := by
    intro k hk; rw [ Nat.pow_succ' ] ; rw [ ← Nat.mod_add_div ( b * ( b ^ k % p ) ) p ] ; ring;
    norm_num [ Nat.add_mul_div_left _ _ ( by linarith : 0 < p ), Nat.mul_mod, Nat.mul_div_assoc ] ; ring;
  have h_sum_remainder : ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, b * (b ^ k % p) = p * ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, ((b * (b ^ k % p)) / p) + ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, (b ^ (k + 1) % p) := by
    rw [ Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => h_remainder x ( Finset.mem_range.mp hx ) ];
  have h_sum_remainder_shift : ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, (b ^ (k + 1) % p) = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (d + 1), (b ^ k % p) - (b ^ 0 % p) := by
    simp +arith +decide [ Finset.sum_range_succ' ];
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.sum_range_succ ];
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hp ]

/-
For a primitive-root base `b` modulo the prime `p`, the remainders `b^k mod p`,
`0 ≤ k < p-1`, run through all of `{1, …, p-1}`, so their sum is `p(p-1)/2`.
-/
lemma remSum_full (p b : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hpb : ¬ p ∣ b)
    (hord : orderOf (b : ZMod p) = p - 1) :
    remSum p b (p - 1) = p * (p - 1) / 2 := by
  -- Let `T = (Finset.range (p-1)).image (fun k => (b:ZMod p)^k)`. Then `T.card = p - 1` (`Finset.card_image_of_injOn`, `Finset.card_range`).
  have hT_card : Finset.card (Finset.image (fun k => (b : ZMod p) ^ k) (Finset.range (p - 1))) = p - 1 := by
    rw [ Finset.card_image_of_injOn, Finset.card_range ];
    grind +suggestions;
  -- Since `T ⊆ univ.erase 0` and both have card `p - 1`, `T = univ.erase 0`.
  have hT_eq : Finset.image (fun k => (b : ZMod p) ^ k) (Finset.range (p - 1)) = Finset.univ.erase 0 := by
    refine' Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le ( Finset.image_subset_iff.mpr _ ) _;
    · simp_all +decide [ ← ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff ];
    · simp_all +decide [ Finset.card_univ ];
  -- Therefore, `∑ x ∈ T, x.val = ∑ x ∈ univ.erase 0, x.val = (∑ x : ZMod p, x.val) - x.val 0 = ∑ x : ZMod p, x.val`.
  have h_sum_T : ∑ x ∈ Finset.image (fun k => (b : ZMod p) ^ k) (Finset.range (p - 1)), x.val = ∑ x : ZMod p, x.val := by
    rw [ hT_eq, ← Finset.sum_erase_add _ _ ( Finset.mem_univ 0 ), add_comm ] ; aesop;

  · rw [ Finset.sum_image ];
    · exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => by erw [ ← ZMod.val_natCast ] ; norm_num;
    · grind;
  · -- Since `ZMod p` is a finite field, its elements are exactly the integers from `0` to `p-1`.

      exact ⟨ fun ⟨ a, ha ⟩ => ha ▸ ZMod.val_lt a, fun hx => ⟨ x, ZMod.val_cast_of_lt hx ⟩ ⟩;
    have h_sum_range : ∑ x ∈ Finset.range p, x = p * (p - 1) / 2 := by

    rw [ ← ZMod.val_natCast, Nat.cast_pow, ← hord, pow_orderOf_eq_one, ZMod.val_one ]

    convert remSum_full p b hpb hord using 1;

  rw [orderOf_eq_iff (by norm_num)]

  have := digitSum_full_period 7 3 (by norm_num) (by norm_num) (by decide)
    orderOf_three_zmod_seven
  simpa using this

quadratic-residue theory is needed once the `-1` square-root observation is made — that
was the unlocking simplification.

Critique (Critic): Hypotheses are all load-bearing: `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` is what makes
`(p-1)/4` integral and the pairing exact; `ord = (p-1)/2` is what makes `b^{(p-1)/4} ≠ 1`.
The statement is not vacuous — witnesses exist (`p=5, b=4`).

Synthesis (PI): Clean statement `digitSum_half_period`, fully proved.
-/

namespace DigitSumHalfPeriod

open Finset

/-- The sum of the base-`b` digits of one period (of length `d`) of `1/p`.
The `k`-th digit is `⌊b·(b^k mod p) / p⌋`. -/
def digitSum (p b d : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, (b * (b ^ k % p)) / p

/-- The sum of the successive remainders `b^k mod p` over one period of length `d`. -/
def remSum (p b d : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, b ^ k % p

/-
Telescoping identity: `p·(digit sum) + (remainder sum) = b·(remainder sum)`,
using `b·r_k = p·a_{k+1} + r_{k+1}` and the fact that the remainders return to `r_0`
after a full period (`b^d ≡ 1`).
-/
lemma digitSum_remSum (p b d : ℕ) (hp : 1 < p) (hd : b ^ d % p = 1) :
    p * digitSum p b d + remSum p b d = b * remSum p b d := by
  unfold digitSum remSum;
  -- By definition of $rem_k$, we have $b * rem_k = p * a_k + rem_{k+1}$.
  have h_remainder : ∀ k < d, b * (b ^ k % p) = p * ((b * (b ^ k % p)) / p) + (b ^ (k + 1) % p) := by
    intro k hk; rw [ Nat.pow_succ' ] ; rw [ ← Nat.mod_add_div ( b * ( b ^ k % p ) ) p ] ; ring;
    norm_num [ Nat.add_mul_div_left _ _ ( by linarith : 0 < p ), Nat.mul_mod, Nat.mul_div_assoc ] ; ring;
  have h_sum_remainder : ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, b * (b ^ k % p) = p * ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, ((b * (b ^ k % p)) / p) + ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, (b ^ (k + 1) % p) := by
    rw [ Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => h_remainder x ( Finset.mem_range.mp hx ) ];
  have h_sum_remainder_shift : ∑ k ∈ Finset.range d, (b ^ (k + 1) % p) = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (d + 1), (b ^ k % p) - (b ^ 0 % p) := by
    simp +arith +decide [ Finset.sum_range_succ' ];
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.sum_range_succ ];
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hp ]

/-
The central algebraic fact: for `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` prime and `b` of multiplicative order
`(p-1)/2`, one has `(b : ZMod p) ^ ((p-1)/4) = -1`.
-/
lemma pow_quarter_eq_negOne (p b : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hp : p.Prime)
    (hpb : ¬ p ∣ b) (h4 : p % 4 = 1)
    (hord : orderOf (b : ZMod p) = (p - 1) / 2) :
    (b : ZMod p) ^ ((p - 1) / 4) = -1 := by
  -- Let $e = (p-1)/4$ and $d = (p-1)/2$. Since $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ and $p \geq 1$, we have $4 \mid (p-1)$ and $d = 2e$ (both provable by `omega`).
  set e : ℕ := (p - 1) / 4
  set d : ℕ := (p - 1) / 2
  have hde : d = 2 * e := by
    omega;
  -- By `mul_self_eq_one_iff`, `x = 1 ∨ x = -1`.
  have h_cases : (b : ZMod p) ^ e = 1 ∨ (b : ZMod p) ^ e = -1 := by
    have h_cases : (b : ZMod p) ^ (2 * e) = 1 := by
      rw [ ← hde, ← hord, pow_orderOf_eq_one ];
    exact eq_or_eq_neg_of_sq_eq_sq _ _ <| by linear_combination' h_cases;
  refine h_cases.resolve_left fun h => ?_;
  have := orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one.mpr h; simp_all +decide ;
  exact Nat.not_dvd_of_pos_of_lt ( Nat.div_pos ( Nat.le_sub_one_of_lt ( by contrapose! hpb; interval_cases p <;> trivial ) ) zero_lt_four ) ( lt_mul_of_one_lt_left ( Nat.div_pos ( Nat.le_sub_one_of_lt ( by contrapose! hpb; interval_cases p <;> trivial ) ) zero_lt_four ) ( by decide ) ) this

/-
Shifting the exponent by a quarter period negates the remainder:
`b^{k + (p-1)/4} mod p = p - (b^k mod p)`.
-/
lemma rem_shift (p b : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hpb : ¬ p ∣ b) (k : ℕ)
    (hK : (b : ZMod p) ^ ((p - 1) / 4) = -1) :
    b ^ (k + (p - 1) / 4) % p = p - b ^ k % p := by
  rw [ ← ZMod.val_natCast, pow_add ];
  simp_all +decide [ ← ZMod.val_natCast ];
  rw [ ZMod.neg_val ];
  simp_all +decide [ ← ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff ]

/-
The remainder sum over one half-period equals `((p-1)/4)·p`, by pairing `k` with
`k + (p-1)/4`.
-/
lemma remSum_eq (p b : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hp : p.Prime) (hpb : ¬ p ∣ b) (h4 : p % 4 = 1)
    (hord : orderOf (b : ZMod p) = (p - 1) / 2) :
    remSum p b ((p - 1) / 2) = (p - 1) / 4 * p := by
  have h_half_period : ∀ k < (p - 1) / 4, b ^ (k + (p - 1) / 4) % p = p - b ^ k % p := by
    intro k hk;
    convert rem_shift p b hpb k _ using 1;
    convert pow_quarter_eq_negOne p b hp hpb h4 hord using 1;
  -- By pairing each term in the first half with its corresponding term in the second half, we can see that each pair sums to $p$.
  have h_pair_sum : ∀ k < (p - 1) / 4, b ^ k % p + b ^ (k + (p - 1) / 4) % p = p := by
    exact fun k hk => by rw [ h_half_period k hk, add_tsub_cancel_of_le ( Nat.le_of_lt ( Nat.mod_lt _ hp.pos ) ) ] ;
  -- By pairing each term in the first half with its corresponding term in the second half, we can see that each pair sums to $p$. Therefore, the sum of all terms in the first half is equal to the sum of all terms in the second half.
  have h_sum_eq : ∑ k ∈ Finset.range ((p - 1) / 2), b ^ k % p = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range ((p - 1) / 4), (b ^ k % p + b ^ (k + (p - 1) / 4) % p) := by
    rw [ show ( p - 1 ) / 2 = ( p - 1 ) / 4 + ( p - 1 ) / 4 by omega, Finset.sum_range_add ] ; simp +arith +decide [ Finset.sum_add_distrib ] ;
  exact h_sum_eq.trans ( by rw [ Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => h_pair_sum x ( Finset.mem_range.mp hx ) ] ; simp +decide )

/-
**Main theorem.** Let `p` be a prime and `b ≥ 2` with `p ∤ b`.  If the multiplicative
order of `b` modulo `p` is `(p-1)/2` and `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, then the sum of the base-`b`
digits of one period of `1/p` equals `(b-1)(p-1)/4`.
-/
theorem digitSum_half_period (p b : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hb : 2 ≤ b)
    (hpb : ¬ p ∣ b) (h4 : p % 4 = 1)
    (hord : orderOf (b : ZMod p) = (p - 1) / 2) :
    digitSum p b ((p - 1) / 2) = (b - 1) * (p - 1) / 4 := by
  haveI := Fact.mk hp
  -- From `digitSum_remSum` and `remSum_eq`, we get `p * D + S = b * S` and `S = ((p-1)/4) * p`.
  have h_eq : p * digitSum p b ((p - 1) / 2) + ((p - 1) / 4) * p = b * ((p - 1) / 4) * p := by
    convert digitSum_remSum p b ( ( p - 1 ) / 2 ) hp.one_lt _ using 1;
    · rw [ remSum_eq p b hp hpb h4 hord ];
    · rw [ mul_assoc, remSum_eq p b hp hpb h4 hord ];
    · rw [ ← ZMod.val_natCast, Nat.cast_pow, ← hord, pow_orderOf_eq_one, ZMod.val_one ];
  rw [ Nat.div_eq_of_eq_mul_left ];
  rw [ Nat.div_eq_of_eq_mul_left ];
  all_goals norm_num;
  any_goals exact ( p - 1 ) / 2;
  · rcases p with ( _ | _ | _ | p ) <;> simp_all +decide;
    cases b <;> norm_num at * ; nlinarith [ Nat.div_mul_cancel ( show 4 ∣ p + 1 + 1 from Nat.dvd_of_mod_eq_zero ( by omega ) ) ];
  · rw [ Nat.div_mul_cancel ( even_iff_two_dvd.mp ( hp.even_sub_one <| by aesop_cat ) ) ]

/-! ## Concrete instances

Each instance discharges the multiplicative-order hypothesis via `orderOf_eq_iff` and a
finite `decide` check, then applies `digitSum_half_period`. -/

/-- Order of `4` modulo `5` is `2 = (5-1)/2`. -/
lemma orderOf_four_zmod_five : orderOf (4 : ZMod 5) = 2 := by
  rw [orderOf_eq_iff (by norm_num)]
  refine ⟨by decide, by decide⟩

/-- Order of `4` modulo `13` is `6 = (13-1)/2`. -/
lemma orderOf_four_zmod_thirteen : orderOf (4 : ZMod 13) = 6 := by
  rw [orderOf_eq_iff (by norm_num)]
  refine ⟨by decide, by decide⟩

/-- The base-`4` digits of one period of `1/5` sum to `3` (`= (4-1)(5-1)/4`). -/
theorem digitSum_five_four : digitSum 5 4 ((5 - 1) / 2) = 3 := by
  have := digitSum_half_period 5 4 (by norm_num) (by norm_num) (by decide) (by decide)
    orderOf_four_zmod_five
  simpa using this

/-- The base-`4` digits of one period of `1/13` sum to `9` (`= (4-1)(13-1)/4`). -/
theorem digitSum_thirteen_four : digitSum 13 4 ((13 - 1) / 2) = 9 := by
  have := digitSum_half_period 13 4 (by norm_num) (by norm_num) (by decide) (by decide)
    orderOf_four_zmod_thirteen
  simpa using this

end DigitSumHalfPeriod

# Computational Evidence — half-period digit sum of `1/p`

Setup: for a prime `p` and base `b` with `p ∤ b`, the base-`b` expansion of `1/p` is
purely periodic with period `d = ord_p(b)`.  The digit sum of one period is
`D(p,b) = Σ_{k=0}^{d-1} ⌊b·(b^k mod p) / p⌋`.  The claim under study:

> if `d = (p-1)/2` and `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, then `D(p,b) = (b-1)(p-1)/4`.

## 1. Small-case calculations (half-period, `p ≡ 1 mod 4`)

Every row below has `ord_p(b) = (p-1)/2`, `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, `p ∤ b`.
Columns: `p, b, d, D(p,b), (b-1)(p-1)/4`.

```
(5,  4,  2,  3,  3)
(13, 4,  6,  9,  9)
(17, 2,  8,  4,  4)
(29, 4, 14, 21, 21)
(29, 5, 14, 28, 28)
(29, 6, 14, 35, 35)
(37, 3, 18, 18, 18)
(37, 4, 18, 27, 27)
(41, 2, 20, 10, 10)
(41, 5, 20, 40, 40)
```

The computed digit sum matches `(b-1)(p-1)/4` in **every** case.

## 2. Necessity of `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` (counterexample hunt)

Repeating the search with the *same* order condition `ord_p(b) = (p-1)/2` but for
primes `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` breaks the identity.  Columns: `p, b, d, D(p,b), (b-1)(p-1)/4`.

```
(7,  4,  3,  3,  4)     <- mismatch
(11, 3,  5,  4,  5)     <- mismatch
(11, 4,  5,  6,  7)     <- mismatch
(11, 5,  5,  8, 10)     <- mismatch
(19, 4,  9, 12, 13)     <- mismatch
(23, 3, 11,  8, 11)     <- mismatch
(31, 7, 15, 36, 45)     <- mismatch
```

So the residue condition `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` is genuinely load-bearing: it is exactly what
makes `(p-1)/4` an integer and forces the quarter-period power `b^{(p-1)/4} ≡ -1`, which
in turn pairs the remainders `r_k` with `r_{k+(p-1)/4} = p - r_k`.  For `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)`
that pairing is unavailable and the digit sum is smaller.

## 3. Full-reptend companion (`ord_p(b) = p-1`)

For primitive-root bases the digit sum is the maximal `(b-1)(p-1)/2`, e.g.
`p=7, b=3`: `d=6`, `D = 6 = (3-1)(7-1)/2`.  This is the `d = p-1` sibling result and is
also formalized (`DigitSumFullPeriod.digitSum_full_period`).

## 4. OEIS

The half-period digit-sum values `(b-1)(p-1)/4` are not a single fixed integer sequence
(they depend on two parameters).  For fixed `b = 10` and `p` ranging over the relevant
primes the period digit sums of `1/p` connect to the general "digit sum of the repetend of
1/n" family (cf. OEIS A036275 for repetends); no dedicated OEIS entry is required for the
closed form itself, which is elementary once established.

## 5. Method note

All numbers above were produced by direct evaluation in `ℕ` (`#eval`) of the same
`digitSum` definition that appears in the Lean files, and the two representative rows
`(5,4)` and `(13,4)` are additionally machine-checked theorems
(`digitSum_five_four`, `digitSum_thirteen_four`).

# Future Directions — digit sums of periodic base-`b` expansions of `1/p`

Derived from the cycle that established: for a prime `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` and a base `b`
whose multiplicative order modulo `p` is exactly `(p-1)/2`, the digits of one period of
the base-`b` expansion of `1/p` sum to `(b-1)(p-1)/4`; and, for a primitive-root base
(order `p-1`), they sum to `(b-1)(p-1)/2`.

## Conjecture 1 — A single order-indexed digit-sum law

For any prime `p`, any base `b ≥ 2` with `p ∤ b`, and period `d = ord_p(b)`, the digit
sum of one period equals `(b-1)·s/p`, where `s` is the sum of the elements of the cyclic
subgroup generated by `b` in the nonzero residues.  When that subgroup is closed under
negation (equivalently, contains `-1`), the sum `s` is exactly `p·d/2` and the digit sum
collapses to `(b-1)·d/2`.

The key insight is that the digit sum is a *linear image of the remainder-orbit sum*, so
the entire arithmetic of the digits is controlled by a single group-theoretic quantity —
the sum over the orbit — rather than by the digits individually.

Why now? The half-period and full-reptend results are the two extreme instances of this
law (orbit closed under negation), and the negation-closure criterion `-1 ∈ ⟨b⟩` is a
clean, checkable divisibility condition (`2 ∣ ord_p(b)` together with the right residue of
`p`), making the general statement immediately testable across all intermediate orders.

## Conjecture 2 — Midy blocks of arbitrary equal length

Whenever `-1` is a power `b^{d/2}` of the base within one period (`d` even and the
half-power equal to `-1`), splitting the period into two halves yields two blocks whose
digitwise sum is constant `b-1` in every position; consequently the two half-block values
sum to `b^{d/2} - 1`.  More generally, if `b^{d/m} ≡ ζ` runs through the `m`-th roots of
unity, the `m` equal sub-blocks have digitwise column sums that are completely determined.

The key insight is that a root-of-unity relation among the base powers forces an exact
digitwise cancellation pattern, upgrading the classical two-block Midy phenomenon to an
`m`-block phenomenon governed by the order of `b` relative to `d`.

Why now? The `b^{(p-1)/4} = -1` identity that drives the half-period result is precisely
the `m = 2` case; recognizing it as one instance of a root-of-unity family invites the
general `m`-block refinement.

## Conjecture 3 — Average digit value stabilizes at `(b-1)/2`

For the two symmetric regimes above the average digit of one period is exactly `(b-1)/2`
(half-period: `((b-1)(p-1)/4)/((p-1)/2)`; full reptend: `((b-1)(p-1)/2)/(p-1)`).  We
conjecture the average digit of one period of `1/p` in base `b` tends to `(b-1)/2` for
*every* base as `p → ∞`, with a bias term controlled by how far the orbit of `b` is from
being negation-symmetric.

The key insight is that negation symmetry of the remainder orbit is exactly the mechanism
that makes each digit's "complement" also appear, pinning the mean at the central value
`(b-1)/2`.

Why now? Both proved theorems land exactly on average `(b-1)/2`, which is strong evidence
that the mean is a robust invariant and that deviations are a lower-order, measurable
correction rather than noise.

## Conjecture 4 — Residue class dichotomy is sharp

For `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` with `ord_p(b) = (p-1)/2` the digit sum is strictly *less than*
`(b-1)(p-1)/4`, and the exact deficit equals `(b-1)/p` times the difference between the
sum of quadratic residues and `p(p-1)/4`.  Equivalently, the deficit is a rational
multiple of the class number `h(-p)` of the imaginary quadratic field `ℚ(√-p)`.

The key insight is that for `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` the residues in the orbit are *not*
symmetric under negation, and their imbalance is precisely the quantity measured by the
class number through the analytic class-number formula.

Why now? The computational evidence shows a systematic (never random) shortfall for
`p ≡ 3 (mod 4)`; tying that shortfall to `h(-p)` would convert an empirical gap into an
exact arithmetic-geometry statement.

## Conjecture 5 — Digit sums separate primes from Carmichael-like composites

Define the base-`b` "period digit sum" `D(n,b)` for any `n` coprime to `b` using the
period of `1/n`.  We conjecture that the clean closed forms `(b-1)·ord/2` hold for a
composite `n` only in degenerate cases, so that a mismatch between `D(n,b)` and the value
predicted by the order alone is a *witness of compositeness* — a digit-sum analogue of a
Fermat/Euler test.

The key insight is that the closed form relied on `p` being prime (so that `x^2 = 1` has
only the roots `±1`); for composite moduli extra square roots of unity break the pairing,
leaving a detectable digit-sum signature.

Why now? Square roots of unity modulo `n` are the exact obstruction exploited by
Miller–Rabin, so a digit-sum test built on the same obstruction could give a
human-readable primality witness directly from the decimal (or base-`b`) expansion of
`1/n`.

/-- `n : ℕ` is a sum of `m` squares: there is a length-`m` list of naturals whose squares
sum to `n`. -/
def IsSumOfMSquares (m n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ l : List ℕ, l.length = m ∧ (l.map (· ^ 2)).sum = n

/-- **Lagrange + padding.** For `m ≥ 4`, *every* natural number is a sum of `m` squares. -/
theorem all_sum_of_m_squares (m n : ℕ) (hm : 4 ≤ m) : IsSumOfMSquares m n := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c, d, habcd⟩ := Nat.sum_four_squares n
  refine ⟨[a, b, c, d] ++ List.replicate (m - 4) 0, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simp [List.length_replicate]; omega
  · simp [List.map_replicate]; omega

/-- For `m ≥ 4` the set of sums of `m` squares is all of `ℕ`: the constraint is vacuous. -/
theorem sumOfMSquares_eq_univ {m : ℕ} (hm : 4 ≤ m) :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n} = Set.univ := by
  ext n; simp [all_sum_of_m_squares m n hm]

/-- Every perfect square is a sum of `m` squares whenever `m ≥ 1` (one term `k`, rest `0`). -/
theorem square_isSumOfMSquares {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m) (k : ℕ) :
    IsSumOfMSquares m (k ^ 2) := by
  refine ⟨[k] ++ List.replicate (m - 1) 0, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simp [List.length_replicate]; omega
  · simp [List.map_replicate]

/-- For any `m ≥ 1` the set of sums of `m` squares is infinite (it contains every square). -/
theorem sumOfMSquares_set_infinite {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m) :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n}.Infinite := by
  refine Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem (f := fun k => k ^ 2) ?_ ?_
  · intro x y h
    have : x ^ 2 = y ^ 2 := h
    nlinarith [Nat.le_total x y]
  · intro k; exact square_isSumOfMSquares hm k

/-- The abstract analytic input.  A real sequence `a` is *sign oscillating* when it is positive
infinitely often and negative infinitely often.  For `a = λ_{sym^j f}` this is the known
theorem on sign changes of symmetric-power Hecke coefficients over all of `ℕ`. -/
structure SignOscillating (a : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop where
  /-- `a` is positive on an infinite set of indices. -/
  pos_infinite : {n | 0 < a n}.Infinite
  /-- `a` is negative on an infinite set of indices. -/
  neg_infinite : {n | a n < 0}.Infinite

/-- **The collapse theorem.** If `a` oscillates in sign over `ℕ`, then for every `m ≥ 4` it
oscillates in sign over the sums of `m` squares: both the positive and the negative
sub-collections indexed by sums of `m` squares are infinite.  The proof uses that the
representability constraint is vacuous for `m ≥ 4` (`all_sum_of_m_squares`). -/
theorem signChanges_ge_four
    {a : ℕ → ℝ} (h : SignOscillating a) {m : ℕ} (hm : 4 ≤ m) :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ 0 < a n}.Infinite ∧
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ a n < 0}.Infinite := by
  have huniv : ∀ n, IsSumOfMSquares m n := fun n => all_sum_of_m_squares m n hm
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · have hset : {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ 0 < a n} = {n | 0 < a n} := by

  · have hset : {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ a n < 0} = {n | a n < 0} := by

    rw [hset]; exact h.neg_infinite

/-- The alternating sign sequence genuinely oscillates: it is `+1` on the (infinite) evens and

namespace SymPowSignChanges

/-- `n : ℕ` is a sum of `m` squares: there is a length-`m` list of naturals whose squares
sum to `n`. -/
def IsSumOfMSquares (m n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ l : List ℕ, l.length = m ∧ (l.map (· ^ 2)).sum = n

/-- **Lagrange + padding.** For `m ≥ 4`, *every* natural number is a sum of `m` squares. -/
theorem all_sum_of_m_squares (m n : ℕ) (hm : 4 ≤ m) : IsSumOfMSquares m n := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c, d, habcd⟩ := Nat.sum_four_squares n
  refine ⟨[a, b, c, d] ++ List.replicate (m - 4) 0, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simp [List.length_replicate]; omega
  · simp [List.map_replicate]; omega

/-- For `m ≥ 4` the set of sums of `m` squares is all of `ℕ`: the constraint is vacuous. -/
theorem sumOfMSquares_eq_univ {m : ℕ} (hm : 4 ≤ m) :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n} = Set.univ := by
  ext n; simp [all_sum_of_m_squares m n hm]

/-- Every perfect square is a sum of `m` squares whenever `m ≥ 1` (one term `k`, rest `0`). -/
theorem square_isSumOfMSquares {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m) (k : ℕ) :
    IsSumOfMSquares m (k ^ 2) := by
  refine ⟨[k] ++ List.replicate (m - 1) 0, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simp [List.length_replicate]; omega
  · simp [List.map_replicate]

/-- For any `m ≥ 1` the set of sums of `m` squares is infinite (it contains every square). -/
theorem sumOfMSquares_set_infinite {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m) :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n}.Infinite := by
  refine Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem (f := fun k => k ^ 2) ?_ ?_
  · intro x y h
    have : x ^ 2 = y ^ 2 := h
    nlinarith [Nat.le_total x y]
  · intro k; exact square_isSumOfMSquares hm k

/-- The abstract analytic input.  A real sequence `a` is *sign oscillating* when it is positive
infinitely often and negative infinitely often.  For `a = λ_{sym^j f}` this is the known
theorem on sign changes of symmetric-power Hecke coefficients over all of `ℕ`. -/
structure SignOscillating (a : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop where
  /-- `a` is positive on an infinite set of indices. -/
  pos_infinite : {n | 0 < a n}.Infinite
  /-- `a` is negative on an infinite set of indices. -/
  neg_infinite : {n | a n < 0}.Infinite

/-- **The collapse theorem.** If `a` oscillates in sign over `ℕ`, then for every `m ≥ 4` it
oscillates in sign over the sums of `m` squares: both the positive and the negative
sub-collections indexed by sums of `m` squares are infinite.  The proof uses that the
representability constraint is vacuous for `m ≥ 4` (`all_sum_of_m_squares`). -/
theorem signChanges_ge_four
    {a : ℕ → ℝ} (h : SignOscillating a) {m : ℕ} (hm : 4 ≤ m) :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ 0 < a n}.Infinite ∧
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ a n < 0}.Infinite := by
  have huniv : ∀ n, IsSumOfMSquares m n := fun n => all_sum_of_m_squares m n hm
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · have hset : {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ 0 < a n} = {n | 0 < a n} := by
      ext n; simp [huniv n]
    rw [hset]; exact h.pos_infinite
  · have hset : {n | IsSumOfMSquares m n ∧ a n < 0} = {n | a n < 0} := by
      ext n; simp [huniv n]
    rw [hset]; exact h.neg_infinite

/-- A concrete non-vacuous witness: the alternating sign sequence `n ↦ (-1)^n`. -/
def altSign : ℕ → ℝ := fun n => if Even n then 1 else -1

/-- The alternating sign sequence genuinely oscillates: it is `+1` on the (infinite) evens and
`-1` on the (infinite) odds. -/
theorem altSign_oscillating : SignOscillating altSign := by
  constructor
  · refine Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem (f := fun k => 2 * k) ?_ ?_
    · intro x y h; have : 2 * x = 2 * y := h; omega
    · intro k
      have he : Even (2 * k) := ⟨k, by ring⟩
      show 0 < altSign (2 * k)
      simp [altSign, he]
  · refine Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem (f := fun k => 2 * k + 1) ?_ ?_
    · intro x y h; have : 2 * x + 1 = 2 * y + 1 := h; omega
    · intro k
      have ho : ¬ Even (2 * k + 1) := by simp [parity_simps]
      show altSign (2 * k + 1) < 0
      simp [altSign, ho]

/-- The collapse theorem is inhabited: `altSign` changes sign infinitely often over the sums of
`8` squares (and, by the same argument, over sums of any `m ≥ 4` squares). -/
theorem altSign_signChanges_eight :
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares 8 n ∧ 0 < altSign n}.Infinite ∧
    {n | IsSumOfMSquares 8 n ∧ altSign n < 0}.Infinite :=
  signChanges_ge_four altSign_oscillating (by norm_num)

end SymPowSignChanges

# Computational Evidence: sign changes of `sym^j` Hecke coefficients over sums of `m` squares

## 1. The representability constraint collapses for `m ≥ 4`

Lagrange's four-square theorem says every `n ∈ ℕ` is a sum of four squares. Padding
with zeros, every `n` is a sum of `m` squares for every `m ≥ 4`. Small-case check of the
set `S_m = { n : n is a sum of m squares }`:

| `m` | first few non-representable `n` | `S_m = ℕ`? |
|-----|----------------------------------|------------|
| 1   | 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, ...          | no (only squares) |
| 2   | 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, ...       | no (misses `3 mod 4`, etc.) |
| 3   | 7, 15, 23, 28, ... (`4^a(8b+7)`)  | no (Legendre's three-square theorem) |
| 4   | none                              | **yes** (Lagrange) |
| ≥ 4 | none                              | **yes** |

So for every `m ≥ 4` the constraint "`n` is a sum of `m` squares" is vacuous, and the
restricted sign-change problem is *identical* to the unrestricted one. This is the entire
reason the paper's window `2 ≤ m ≤ 12` extends to all even `m ≥ 2`: only `m = 2` (and, for
odd `m`, `m = 1, 3`) is genuinely restrictive.

## 2. The boundary case `m = 2`: residue obstruction

A sum of two squares is never `≡ 3 (mod 4)` (squares are `0` or `1 mod 4`, so `a² + b²` is
`0, 1, 2 mod 4`). Hence `3 ∉ S_2`, so `S_2 ≠ ℕ`. This is the arithmetic reason `m = 2`
requires a genuinely different argument from the collapse.

- Non-representable-by-two-squares (`ℕ \ S_2`): 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 19, 21, 22, 23, ...
  (OEIS A022544).
- Sums of two squares (`S_2`): 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 25, ... (OEIS
  A001481).
- `S_2` is nevertheless infinite (it contains every perfect square `k² = k² + 0²`), which is
  what the sign-change statement needs on the index side.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

The claim to falsify is "for even `m ≥ 4`, sign changes over `S_m` need extra hypotheses
beyond unrestricted oscillation." We searched for an even `m ≥ 4` with `S_m ≠ ℕ`: none exists,
because Lagrange already gives `S_4 = ℕ` and `S_4 ⊆ S_m` for `m ≥ 4`. No counterexample; the
collapse is unconditional for `m ≥ 4`.

## 4. Concrete non-vacuous instance

The alternating sequence `a(n) = (-1)^n` satisfies the abstract oscillation hypothesis
(`+1` on the infinite set of evens, `-1` on the infinite set of odds). Applying the collapse
theorem, `a` changes sign infinitely often over `S_8` (and every `S_m`, `m ≥ 4`), confirming
the machinery is not vacuously true.

# Future Directions: sign changes of symmetric-power coefficients on thin sets

These conjectures grow out of the central finding of this cycle: the constraint "`n` is a sum
of `m` squares" stops binding once `m ≥ 4`, so the interesting arithmetic lives entirely in the
thin sets `m = 1, 2, 3`, where the representable integers form a positive- or zero-density but
strictly proper subset of the naturals.

**Conjecture.** For a normalised Hecke eigenform `f`, every symmetric power `sym^j f`, the
number of sign changes of `λ_{sym^j f}(n)` among sums of two squares up to `X` grows like a
positive power of `X`, with an exponent independent of `j`.

The key insight is that once the ambient set is thin, the sign-change count is governed by the
local density of the thin set rather than by the depth `j` of the symmetric power, because the
oscillation of the coefficients is already "generic" relative to any fixed arithmetic filter.
Why now? The collapse phenomenon isolates `m = 2` as the sole genuinely restrictive even case,
so quantitative sign-change counting can be attacked one thin set at a time instead of across a
whole family of `m`.

## 2. Three-square sets and the Legendre obstruction

**Conjecture.** The sign-change phenomenon persists over sums of *three* squares, i.e. over
`ℕ \ {4^a(8b+7)}`, for every `sym^j f`, even though this set omits an infinite,
positive-density family of integers.

The key insight is that the removed integers `4^a(8b+7)` form a multiplicatively structured,
sign-neutral family, so deleting them cannot destroy an oscillation that is spread across
residue classes. Why now? The two-square boundary case shows that a single residue obstruction
(`3 mod 4`) is compatible with infinitely many sign changes; the three-square case tests whether
the phenomenon survives a *hierarchical* obstruction indexed by powers of four.

## 3. Sign changes over shifted representable sets

**Conjecture.** For every fixed shift `h ≥ 0`, the coefficients `λ_{sym^j f}(n + h)` change
sign infinitely often as `n` ranges over sums of two squares.

The key insight is that shifting the index set by a constant preserves its asymptotic density
while decorrelating it from the multiplicative structure of the coefficients, so the shift
cannot conspire to freeze the sign. Why now? Having reduced the whole even-`m` family to the
single set `S_2`, one can probe robustness by perturbing that set rather than by changing `m`.

## 4. Simultaneous sign changes across symmetric powers

**Conjecture.** For any finite set of exponents `j_1 < ... < j_r`, there are infinitely many
sums of two squares `n` at which all of `λ_{sym^{j_1} f}(n), ..., λ_{sym^{j_r} f}(n)` are
positive, and infinitely many at which all are negative.

The key insight is that the symmetric-power coefficients, viewed as coordinates, equidistribute
against the Sato–Tate measure jointly, so any prescribed sign pattern occurs with positive
frequency even after restricting to a thin representable set. Why now? The collapse result makes
the ambient set uniform across all `m ≥ 4`, focusing attention on *joint* behaviour of the
coefficients rather than on the representability index.

## 5. A `sum-of-m-squares` threshold theorem for general oscillating multiplicative data

**Conjecture.** Any real multiplicative sequence that is unbounded in both signs changes sign
infinitely often over sums of `m` squares for every `m ≥ 4`, with no arithmetic hypothesis on
the sequence beyond two-sided unboundedness.

set, so it should transfer *any* two-sided oscillation — automorphic or not — from `ℕ` to the
representable set. Why now? The present cycle proves exactly this transfer for the abstract
`SignOscillating` interface; the conjecture asks how far the interface can be weakened while
retaining the conclusion.

    Finset (Fin n × Fin n × Fin n × Fin n) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun q => q.1 < q.2.1 ∧ q.2.2.1 < q.2.2.2 ∧

  rw [show boundary3 (Finsupp.single tetra0 (1 : ZMod 2)) = bdGen tetra0 from by simp [boundary3]]
  intro h
  have hcoef := congrArg (fun f => f (tetra0.erase ((0, 0) : Cell 5))) h
  simp only [Finsupp.coe_zero, Pi.zero_apply] at hcoef
  rw [bdGen, Finsupp.finset_sum_apply] at hcoef
  rw [Finset.sum_eq_single ((0, 0) : Cell 5)] at hcoef
  · rw [Finsupp.single_eq_same] at hcoef
    exact one_ne_zero hcoef
  · intro b hb hbne
    rw [Finsupp.single_apply, if_neg]
    intro herase
    apply hbne
    by_contra hne
    have hmem : b ∈ tetra0.erase ((0, 0) : Cell 5) := Finset.mem_erase.mpr ⟨hne, hb⟩
    rw [← herase] at hmem
    exact (notMem_erase b tetra0) hmem

    exact absurd (by decide : ((0, 0) : Cell 5) ∈ tetra0) hnotin

requested `rank ∂₃ = 6·I(cyc 5) = 0`. -/
theorem boundary3_map_ne_zero : (boundary3 : _ →ₗ[ZMod 2] (Finset (Cell 5) →₀ ZMod 2)) ≠ 0 := by
  intro h
  apply boundary3_ne_zero
  rw [h]; rfl

# Computational Evidence: Latin Square Graphs, Regularity, and Intercalates

All computations below were run directly with `#eval` in Lean over exact
finite types (`Fin n`), so the numbers are exact, not floating point.

## 1. Degree of the Latin square graph `L(M)`

For the cyclic Latin square `M i j = i + j`, the degree of a fixed cell is:

| n | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| deg | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 |

This matches `3(n-1)` exactly. The general theorem
`LatinSquare.neighbors_card` proves `deg = 3(n-1)` for **every** Latin square, by
partitioning the neighbourhood into the co-row, co-column, and co-symbol blocks
(each of size `n-1`), whose disjointness is exactly the Latin property.

## 2. Number of cells carrying a fixed symbol

| n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| #cells with symbol s | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

Always `n`, confirming the co-symbol block has size `n-1` after removing the base
cell (used in `LatinSquare.symSet_card`).

## 3. Intercalate counts of the cyclic Latin square

An intercalate is a `2×2` Latin subsquare (rows `r₁<r₂`, cols `c₁<c₂` with the
crossed pattern). Counts for `M i j = i+j`:

| n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I(M) | 0 | 1 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 9 | 0 | 16 |

Pattern: `I = (n/2)²` for even `n`, and `I = 0` for odd `n`. The half-shift
`m = n/2` is the unique nonzero solution of `2(c₁-c₂) = 0` in `Z_n`, which is why
odd orders have none. The existence direction (even `n` ⇒ an intercalate exists)
is proved in `Cyclic.lean` as `cyclicLatin_intercalate_even`.

- OEIS: the even-order subsequence `1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …` is `A000290` (squares);
  the full interleaved sequence `0,1,0,4,0,9,0,16,…` is the squares placed at even
  indices.

## 4. Consistency check for the homology dimension formula

The research target claims `dim H₂ = (n-1)³ - I(M)`. A necessary sanity condition
is `I(M) ≤ (n-1)³` (a dimension is non-negative). The maximum number of
intercalates over all Latin squares of order `n` is at most `n²(n-1)/4`
(each unordered row pair contributes at most `n/2` intercalates, from the 2-cycles
of the permutation linking the two rows). Since
`n²(n-1)/4 ≤ (n-1)³ ⟺ n² ≤ 4(n-1)² ⟺ n ≤ 2(n-1) ⟺ n ≥ 2`,
the RHS is non-negative for all `n ≥ 2`, consistent with being a dimension. The
cyclic square realizes only `(n/2)²`, far below this maximum.

## 5. Tetrahedra hunt

For each intercalate, the four cells are pairwise adjacent (a `K₄`), and the two
diagonal edges are *symbol* edges connecting cells in different rows and columns.
Checked on the order-4 and order-6 cyclic squares: every intercalate yields such a
mixed `K₄`, and no `K₄` of this mixed diagonal type occurs without an intercalate.
This is the local mechanism behind the `-I(M)` term and is proved in generality by
`Intercalate.forms_clique` and `Intercalate.diagonal_is_symbol_edge`.

# Future Directions: Homology of Latin Square Graphs

These conjectures are distilled from the current cycle's findings on the clique
structure of Latin square graphs. Each is falsifiable and, we believe, timely.

## 1. The intercalate-corrected second Betti number

**Conjecture.** For every Latin square `M` of order `n ≥ 5`, the second homology of
the clique complex of its associated strongly regular graph has dimension exactly
`(n-1)³ - I(M)` over any field, where `I(M)` is the number of intercalates.

The key insight is that each intercalate is a "hidden" tetrahedron whose two
diagonal edges are realized only by the symbol relation, not by shared rows or
columns; filling this tetrahedron cancels exactly one otherwise-independent
2-cycle, so the second Betti number decreases by one per intercalate while the
line-cliques contribute the uniform `(n-1)³` bulk.

Why now? The uniform bulk term is a property of the strongly regular parameters
`(n², 3(n-1), n, 6)`, which are identical across all Latin squares of a given
order; the only combinatorial invariant left to explain the variation in topology
is the intercalate count, and recent enumerations of intercalate distributions
make the corrective term both computable and testable at scale.

## 2. Field-independence of the clique homology

**Conjecture.** The Betti numbers of the clique complex of a Latin square graph are
independent of the coefficient field; equivalently, its integral homology is
torsion-free in degrees up to two.

The key insight is that the tetrahedra created by intercalates attach along full
triangular faces already present from the line-cliques, so the boundary maps admit
a basis in which they are represented by totally unimodular incidence patterns,
which forces the vanishing of torsion.

Why now? Torsion in flag complexes of highly symmetric graphs has recently been
found to appear only through "twisted" attachments; Latin square graphs are a
natural stress test because their tetrahedra attach in the untwisted, transversal
manner, so a torsion-free verdict would sharply delimit where torsion can occur.

## 3. Extremal topology and the intercalate spectrum

**Conjecture.** Among all Latin squares of order `n`, the maximizers of the second
Betti number are exactly the intercalate-free (`N∞`) squares, and the minimizers
are exactly the squares of maximum intercalate count; both extremes are attained
and the Betti number is a strictly decreasing function of intercalate count.

The key insight is that intercalate count is not merely correlated with but
functionally determines the homology, so extremal topology and extremal
combinatorics coincide: topological complexity is maximized precisely when the
`2×2` subsquare structure is most rigid.

Why now? Intercalate-free Latin squares are known to exist for all orders above a
small threshold, and their asymptotic density is now understood, so the two ends of
the spectrum can be exhibited explicitly and compared.

## 4. A homological detector for main-class equivalence

**Conjecture.** Two Latin squares whose graphs have isomorphic clique complexes
have equal intercalate counts, and within a fixed order the graded Betti sequence
separates species that share the strongly regular parameters but differ in
intercalate structure.

The key insight is that clique homology promotes the single number `I(M)` to a
graded invariant that survives graph isomorphism, giving a topological shadow of
the notoriously subtle main-class classification of Latin squares.

Why now? The number of species grows super-exponentially and current invariants
saturate quickly; a topological invariant computable from local `2×2` data offers a
fresh and scalable separating statistic.

## 5. Higher intercalates and higher homology

**Conjecture.** For each `k ≥ 2`, the dimension of the `k`-th clique homology of a
Latin square graph is a fixed polynomial in `n` corrected by a signed count of
`k`-dimensional "Latin sub-configurations" (nested intercalate patterns), extending
the degree-two formula `(n-1)³ - I(M)`.

The key insight is that the degree-two correction by intercalates is the first
instance of a general principle: every homological degree is governed by the
enumeration of a correspondingly higher-order Latin subpattern that closes an
otherwise-open cycle.

Why now? The degree-two case links a clean topological quantity to the single most
studied Latin square statistic; establishing the pattern one degree higher would
turn a scattered set of enumeration problems into a single homological hierarchy.
